consensus_summary: Egypt conventionally symbolizes bondage to sin, oppressive worldly power, and the realm from which God redeems his people through an exodus.
book_summary: Egypt is identified specifically with apostate Jerusalem, understood as the prophet-killing great city and the whore/Babylon of Revelation.
consensus_core_identification: Egypt = bondage to sin and the oppressive world-system.
book_core_identification: Egypt = apostate Jerusalem, identified with prophetic Babylon.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus applies the symbol broadly to spiritual bondage and worldly oppression, while the book elevates one acknowledged contextual possibility—unfaithful Jerusalem in Revelation 11:8—into the controlling identification and links it to Babylon. This excludes or displaces the wider Exodus-based application as the term’s core meaning.
material_contradiction: The book replaces an abstract spiritual condition or world-system with a specific covenant city. Although Jerusalem can exemplify bondage and opposition to God, identifying Egypt as Jerusalem is not equivalent to identifying it as bondage to sin generally.
rationale: The reading is not novel because the consensus explicitly recognizes that Revelation 11:8 may apply spiritual Egypt to unfaithful Jerusalem. Nevertheless, the book does more than narrow the conventional meaning: it makes Jerusalem/Babylon the symbol’s central referent and presents the standard bondage/world-system reading only as the common view. Thus it reclassifies a contextual alternative as the primary identification and replaces the consensus core.
strongest_objection: Revelation 11:8 strongly points to Jerusalem as the city spiritually called Egypt, and the other verses establish Jerusalem as being in bondage, likened to Sodom, and guilty of killing prophets. But the printed citations do not explicitly identify the Babylon of Revelation 17–18 with Jerusalem, nor do they show that Egypt generally signifies Jerusalem rather than carrying the broader Exodus-based bondage symbolism.
